A gravitational lens forms when a massive object, such as a galaxy cluster, lies between an observer and a distant source. The mass curves spacetime, bending the paths of light rays so that the source appears distorted, magnified, or multiply imaged. The degree of magnification depends on the alignment and on the mass distribution of the lens; near critical curves, magnification can exceed a factor of ten, allowing astronomers to detect galaxies that would otherwise be too faint. To use a lens quantitatively, researchers build a mass model constrained by the positions of multiply imaged features, then invert it to reconstruct the source's true shape. Uncertainties in the model, particularly in the distribution of dark matter, propagate directly into the inferred brightness and size of the background galaxy, which is why independent constraints from spectroscopy and weak lensing are essential.
